Hi Alex — great conversation today, thanks for the time. Recap of the performance / SLO items we covered and suggested next steps: 

Summary (from today)
- Target P95 latency: 200 ms (inbound inference requests)
- Sustained throughput: ~800 qps during business hours
- Burst profile: up to 2000 qps for spikes lasting 1–3 minutes
- Concurrency: typical per-request concurrency spikes; need to support up to 1,500 concurrent requests at peak
- Streaming: low-TPS streaming (voice transcription) with strict tail latency requirements for partial transcripts

Key constraints we heard
- Pulling cold-starts will hurt the P95 objective (you emphasized tail behavior matters more than average)
- Burst traffic is spikey but short-lived — prefer fast scale-up and a warm pool pre-warmed to serve initial burst

What we recommend / options to meet 200 ms P95
- Warm pool: maintain pre-warmed instances with model loaded and KV cache primed for top request prefixes
- Concurrency per GPU: start with 8 concurrent request slots per GPU (depends on model/quantization)
- Autoscale policy: aggressive scale-up (provision additional warm instances) with short queue window and token-level prioritization for streaming requests
- Fallbacks: configure a dedicated burst capacity tier (reserved capacity) if you need hard SLOs during sustained bursts

Next steps / action items
- I attached our SLO questionnaire (slo-qualification-sheet.xlsx) — please fill traffic shapes and tail-latency histograms where available
- Dev will send a short technical note on warm-pool behavior and scale-up latencies (cc'd: Dev Patel)
- Schedule a technical deep dive to validate config and run a small load test (proposed: Tue May 18 10:00 AM PT) — I will send a calendar invite

Attachments: slo-qualification-sheet.xlsx, redwood-autoscale-playbook.pdf

Thanks — happy to sync more if anything above doesn't match what you intended.

Hi Alex — quick technical note on warm pools and scale-up behavior to help interpret what Marissa outlined. TL;DR: warm pool = instances with model loaded and runtime process up; cold start = provisioning infra + loading weights + kernel warmup.

Details:
- Warm pool contents: model checkpoints loaded to GPU memory, runtime process up, and (optionally) KV cache primed for common prefixes if you supply representative prefix lists. Warm instances can accept requests immediately once CPU/GPU schedulers assign work.
- Typical times:
  - Cold start (new VM/container + load model): ~8–20s depending on model size and infra (we can quantify per-model)
  - From warm pool: instance ready -> can accept first request in ~50–300 ms (network latency + runtime scheduling)
  - If KV cache primed for that prefix, first-token latency is closer to the lower bound (50–120 ms)
- Autoscaler behavior:
  - Aggressive scale policy: detect sustained queueing or CPU/GPU saturation and spin up additional warm instances in parallel
  - Queueing window: we keep a short queue (~200–400 ms target) before provisioning; requests may be queued for that window to avoid over-provisioning for micro-spikes
  - Burst capacity: we can reserve a warm pool sized for expected 99th percentile bursts. For very hard SLOs we recommend a small reserved capacity commitment (dedicated) to cover worst-case bursts
- Concurrency guidance:
  - Start with 8 concurrent request slots per A100-like GPU for chat/text models; adjust based on model and quantization. More concurrency reduces GPU efficiency and can increase tail latency if oversubscribed.

Recommendation to meet 200 ms P95 with your profile
- Maintain at least 3 warm instances per region (model-dependent) to cover initial burst while autoscaler provisions more
- Prime KV cache for top 20 prefixes from your traffic sample (we can help extract these)
- Use short queue window + aggressive parallel provisioning to bring scale-up latency < 1s for most bursts
- If you require hard guarantees for 3-minute sustained spikes to 2,000 qps, consider a small reserved burst pool (we can size that once we see the filled SLO sheet)

I attached our autoscale playbook (redwood-autoscale-playbook.pdf) and linked an internal runbook: https://redwood.app/runbooks/autoscale-playbook

Happy to walk through these numbers in the tech deep-dive — I can demonstrate a small load test showing warm-pool vs cold-start behavior.
